item.title: Is your memory lying to you?
item.description: Vivid memories are not more accurate. The clarity of a memory does not correlate with its factual consistency. Your most intense recollections are just as prone to decay as your mundane ones. The evidence shows that while flashbulb memories feel more accurate and vivid than everyday memories, they do not actually maintain higher levels of consistency over time.

item.title: Who is more persuasive: you or a machine?
item.description: An ai model can match or exceed human experts in persuasion. In some cases, the persuasive impact of gpt-4 rivaled and even surpassed that of human experts. The evidence shows that LLMs possess significant persuasive capabilities that can match or beat humans in specific contexts, but they are not yet more effective at large-scale distribution than traditional methods.

item.title: Does social rejection feel like a physical wound?
item.description: Social rejection may not use the same pain matrix. While social pain and physical pain share psychological consequences, research fails to confirm they use the same primary pain matrix. The evidence shows that social and physical pain share psychological outcomes and some brain regions, but significant research fails to confirm they use the same primary pain matrix.

item.title: Why does your brain prioritize others?
item.description: Your brain has a specific circuit for learning only when acting for others. Activity in the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex and basal forebrain drives learning specifically in prosocial contexts. The evidence identifies specific neural circuits and evolutionary mechanisms for prosociality but shows that these behaviors are not uniform and are influenced by external factors like socioeconomic status.

item.title: Does shared trauma actually create a bond?
item.description: Depression, not trauma, is the primary driver of bonding failure. Postpartum depression at 2 months after delivery is a more important factor affecting bonding failure than posttraumatic stress symptoms after childbirth. The evidence is mixed and shows associations rather than direct causation. The sources indicate that bonding impairment is more consistently associated with maternal depression and specific types of childhood neglect than with the direct experience of trauma.

item.title: Does your best friend affect your romance?
item.description: Friendship jealousy is a defense against replacement. Research shows you feel jealousy specifically when a third party threatens your position in a friendship. This behavior is a tool to counter that threat. The sources confirm that friendship jealousy exists as a response to being replaced by a third party, but they do not provide direct evidence that a 'best friend' specifically decreases romantic relationship quality.

item.title: Does sugar really make children hyperactive?
item.description: Ultra-processed foods impact cognition more than sugar. While sugar does not affect behavior or cognitive performance in children, a combination of ultra-processed foods consistently shows the strongest negative effects across most cognitive domains. The evidence confirms that sugar does not affect children's behavior or cognition, though other ultra-processed foods may have negative cognitive effects.

item.title: Who funded your heart health advice?
item.description: The sugar industry funded research to cast doubt on sucrose hazards. During the 1960s and 1970s, industry-sponsored programs successfully promoted fat as the primary cause of coronary heart disease while downplaying the risks of sugar. The evidence shows that the sugar industry actively funded and influenced research to downplay the risks of sucrose and shift the blame for heart disease toward fat.

item.title: Are you sober when you are tired?
item.description: Your tired brain mirrors a drunk one. After 20-25 hours of wakefulness, your performance decrements can equal a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10%. The evidence shows that sleep deprivation causes significant cognitive and motor impairments that can match alcohol intoxication, but the severity of these effects is task-dependent and may be overestimated in some studies.

item.title: What happens when a species disappears forever?
item.description: We may have already lost 7% of the species on Earth. Extrapolation from a random sample of land snail species suggests 130,000 extinctions have already occurred. The evidence indicates that vertebrate species and genera are being lost at rates far exceeding natural background levels, though the total number of known extinctions remains low.

item.title: Why do the poorest people play the most?
item.description: Low income fuels the highest lottery participation. People with the least money play the most. They pay a regressive tax on games that cost them more relative to their income. The evidence consistently shows that lower-income individuals participate more in lotteries and face a regressive tax burden, though higher-priced games may be less regressive.

item.title: Does your child know why they want that snack?
item.description: Knowing how advertising works does not protect children. Understanding the tactics of marketing fails to shield children from its impact on their brand and product attitudes. The evidence consistently shows that exposure to unhealthy food marketing leads to increased dietary intake and influences preferences in children.

item.title: Where do you go when your phone dies?
item.description: Your brain is losing its internal map. Heavy GPS use is linked to a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory and reduced brain connectivity. The evidence shows a correlation between high GPS usage and poorer spatial memory and reduced hippocampal connectivity, but it does not prove that GPS use causes a loss of navigation skills.

item.title: Why does a lie reach you before the truth?
item.description: Falsehoods diffuse farther and faster than truth. False news spreads more broadly and deeper than the truth in every category of information. You are moving through a landscape where lies travel with more speed than facts. The evidence confirms that false news spreads more effectively than truth due to human behavior and novelty, though people are generally capable of discerning falsehoods.

item.title: What did you miss in the last hour?
item.description: You do not notice large changes in your visual field. People often fail to notice significant changes in visual scenes, even when those changes happen right in front of their eyes. The evidence confirms that people frequently fail to notice significant changes in scenes, though these failures can be mitigated by increased attention or saliency.

item.title: Are you actually learning the material?
item.description: Removing AI access causes a 17% grade drop. Students who used GPT-4 perform worse than those who never had access. This result is mixed and depends on how the tool is used. The evidence shows that AI can improve immediate performance and proficiency, but without proper guardrails or pedagogical design, it can hinder the actual acquisition of skills.

item.title: Will you stay still or step in?
item.description: Danger makes people act. Bystanders were 19 times more likely to intervene in real-life conflicts when danger was present than when it was not. The evidence is mixed. The evidence shows that while the 'bystander effect' exists, it is significantly mitigated by the presence of danger and specific situational factors.

item.title: Is a classic psychiatry study a lie?
item.description: Rosenhan's research may be scientific fraud. Recent evidence identifies the study as a successful case of scientific fraud. The evidence is conflicted, with one source explicitly labeling the study as fraud while another study disputes the conclusions of a modern critic who used Rosenhan's work as a basis.

item.title: Is your screen actually hurting your mind?
item.description: Evidence for social media impact is often weak. Most reviews interpret the associations between social media use and mental health as weak or inconsistent. The evidence shows a complex picture where some specific types of social media use are linked to mental health problems, but the overall evidence is often weak or inconclusive.

item.title: Who will you call tonight?
item.description: Poor social relationships are as deadly as light smoking. Research shows the risk of mortality from poor social relationships is similar to the risk from light smoking. It also exceeds the risks from hypertension and obesity. The evidence consistently shows that poor social relationships and isolation are significant predictors of mortality across various demographics and health conditions.

item.title: Is your confidence a result of your environment?
item.description: East Asians do not self-enhance. While Westerners show a clear self-serving bias, this behavior is notably absent in East Asian cultures. The evidence on this is mixed due to measurement limitations. The evidence shows that self-enhancement is a common human phenomenon but is not universal, as it is notably absent in East Asian cultures.

item.title: Does giving money actually cure depression?
item.description: Cash transfers do not significantly reduce depressive symptoms. While 85% of interventions showed some positive impact on mental health outcomes in children, the evidence shows no significant impact on depressive symptoms specifically. The evidence shows that financial strain and debt are linked to mental health problems, but the impact of financial interventions on specific symptoms like depression can be inconsistent.

item.title: Does stress always change your brain?
item.description: Chronic stress does not always shrink your brain. While some studies show reduced hippocampal volume, others show no effect or even volume increases in resilient subjects. The evidence is mixed, showing that chronic stress can reduce hippocampal volume in some contexts but does not consistently cause it across all subjects or conditions.

item.title: Why do you forget what you just searched?
item.description: Your knowledge base determines your memory loss. People with a larger knowledge base are less susceptible to the consequences of internet use than those with a smaller knowledge base. The evidence confirms that internet use impacts memory mechanisms, but it also shows that individual knowledge levels and specific behaviors moderate these effects.

item.title: Does the city sound hurt your heart?
item.description: Road noise is linked to cardiovascular risks. Studies show a positive association between transportation noise and risks like arterial hypertension. However, some meta-analyses find the link to ischemic heart disease to be statistically insignificant. The evidence shows a positive association between road traffic noise and cardiovascular risks like hypertension and incident CVD, though the strength and significance of these links vary across different studies.

item.title: How much of the ocean floor have you actually seen?
item.description: You have seen less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor. The area we have visually observed is approximately a tenth of the size of Belgium. Most of the rest remains unseen. The evidence confirms that direct visual observation of the deep seafloor is extremely limited and heavily skewed toward specific nations.

item.title: Does more money actually make you happier?
item.description: The data on your happiness is contested. Some studies show well-being rises linearly with income for everyone. Others suggest emotional well-being stops improving at $75,000. This depends on how well-being is measured. The evidence is conflicting, with some studies showing a linear increase in well-being for all earners and others identifying a specific plateau for emotional well-being at $75,000.

item.title: Is the air in your room affecting your choices?
item.description: The impact of CO2 on your brain is inconsistent. While some studies show that higher carbon dioxide levels reduce decision-making performance, others show performance can remain similar or even exceed baseline at higher concentrations. The evidence shows that while elevated CO2 is linked to and can cause decrements in decision-making, the effects are inconsistent and may vary depending on the specific concentration and subject population.

item.title: Who is funding the science you read?
item.description: The tobacco industry deliberately alters knowable facts for profit. Research shows they misrepresent empirical evidence to promote their own agenda. They create front organizations to obscure their involvement in science. The sources provide consistent evidence that the tobacco industry employs diverse, systematic strategies to manufacture doubt and influence regulations for profit.

item.title: Is your head moving faster through time than your feet?
item.description: Time passes faster at your head than at your feet. Clocks at a higher gravitational potential tick faster than identical clocks at a lower potential. This difference is detectable over height changes of less than 1 meter. The evidence confirms that clocks at higher gravitational potentials tick faster, with measurements capable of detecting these differences at the centimeter and millimeter scales.

item.title: Does your learning style actually help you learn?
item.description: Only 26% of learning outcome measures show benefits for matched instruction. The evidence is mixed. While some studies show a small benefit, others show no significant relationship between learning style preference and comprehension or aptitude. The evidence is mixed, showing a small positive effect in one meta-analysis but no significant results in experimental studies and a near-zero effect size in another meta-analysis.

item.title: Does watching others make you feel less?
item.description: Passive scrolling causes declines in well-being by increasing envy. While general social media use shows inconsistent links to mental health, specifically watching others without interacting is associated with lower affective well-being. The evidence shows that passive use can specifically harm well-being via envy, but the overall relationship between social media types and mental health is inconsistent across different research methods.

item.title: Who are you spending your hours on?
item.description: Singles invest more in friendships for self-esteem. Greater friendship investment predicts higher friendship quality and self-esteem later on. This association is stronger for single people than for those in partnerships. The evidence shows that time spent together and engagement in activities are associated with closer friendships and higher self-esteem, particularly for single individuals.

item.title: Can you tell who is real?
item.description: AI faces are rated as more trustworthy than real faces. Studies show that synthetic faces are indistinguishable from human ones and earn higher trust ratings. You are more likely to believe a person who does not exist. The evidence confirms that AI faces can be more trustworthy than real ones and that humans currently struggle to detect them at rates better than chance.

item.title: Do you really choose what you buy?
item.description: Nudge effects drop when the intervention is removed. In 68% of studies, choice architecture changed behavior while the intervention was present. This figure falls to 47% once the intervention is removed. The evidence shows that nudges have measurable effects that vary by context, with specific techniques like decision structure performing better than others.

item.title: Does your brain stay clean while you sleep?
item.description: Your brain clears waste during sleep. Natural sleep or anesthesia is associated with a 60% increase in the brain's interstitial space. This process increases the rate of β-amyloid clearance. The evidence shows that sleep is a primary period for glymphatic waste clearance, though specific disorders like sleep apnea and Parkinson's disease are associated with impaired clearance.

item.title: Do you value the art or the artist's struggle?
item.description: You devalue art when you know it is ai-made. People give lower ratings to ai art even when it is indistinguishable from human work. This happens because you perceive less effort in the process. The evidence shows a consistent negative bias toward AI-generated art driven by perceptions of effort and social identification, though this bias is not automatic and can be influenced by specific framing and context.

item.title: Did you evolve from a chimpanzee?
item.description: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor. Evidence from multiple studies shows that humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Instead, both species branched off from a shared ancestor. The sources provide multiple independent methods and models that consistently point to a common ancestor for humans and chimpanzees, though they differ on the specific timing of the divergence.

item.title: How much of what you believe is actually true?
item.description: Only 36% of replicated psychology experiments achieved statistical significance. While 97% of original studies reported statistically significant results, only 36% of the replicated studies achieved the same. The evidence shows a substantial decline in replication success compared to original findings, with many tests appearing to yield negligible effects.

item.title: Does more money always mean more happiness?
item.description: Income and happiness do not always move together. In some parts of the world, the relationship between wealth and well-being becomes negative. This means more money can lead to less happiness in specific regions. The evidence largely contradicts the proposed angle by showing that happiness often does rise with income, though this varies significantly by region.
